texto:
Google has published a help page describing AI-generated review summaries that appear inside Search ads in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and India, pulling positive comments from reviews across the web into the ad text without giving advertisers the ability to edit what is said about them. The page was first reported on October 24, 2026 by PPC News Feed, which credited Hana Kobzová with finding it.
In Short
Google now uses AI to read online reviews of a business and write a short, positive summary that shows up inside that business's Search ad. Advertisers in four English-speaking markets can have this text appear in their ads, but they cannot change the words Google writes. What appears under a business's name in a paid ad is no longer written only by the business itself.
What the help page says
The document, titled "About Review summaries" and filed in the Google Ads Help Center under "Manage ads" and "Add more information to your ad," carries no publication date or last-updated date. It defines the feature in a single sentence. "Review summaries on Search are AI-powered summaries of online reviews that appear directly as part of your Search ads," according to Google. "They highlight positive insights from across the web to help potential customers evaluate your business and build confidence in your offerings."
The page is organised into four sections: benefits, how the summaries work, eligibility and availability, and key considerations. It is short. There is no screenshot of the format, no example of the generated text, no reporting column, and no instruction on how to switch the feature on or off.
How the summaries are produced
The mechanics, as Google describes them, are compact. "Google AI automatically aggregates online reviews from across the web to generate review summaries," according to the help page. "These summaries are positive only, and represent customer experiences and key insights about your business. On Search ads, review summaries appear as short AI-generated commentary."
On accuracy, the page offers one sentence: "All summaries are generated using responsible AI best practices, including strong grounding requirements to ensure quality and accuracy." Grounding here refers to the technique of tying a language model's output to a set of source documents, in this case reviews, so that the generated text reflects material that exists rather than inventions. Grounding is meant to reduce hallucination, the tendency of large language models to produce fluent statements that are false. The help page does not name the review sources, the threshold for how many reviews a business needs, how recent the reviews must be, or how the system treats a business whose reviews are mostly negative.
That last question is not idle. The page states twice that the output is positive only. In the "Key considerations" section, Google writes: "Review summaries are only positive, highlighting benefits from customer reviews." A summary built only from favourable material is, by construction, a selection rather than a representation of the overall balance of opinion. The page does not say whether a business with a low average rating can still receive a summary drawn from its minority of positive reviews.
Where and when they appear
Eligibility is set out in five lines, according to Google:
- Campaign type: Search campaigns
- Ad placement: All positions on Google.com
- Location and language: US, AU, UK, IN in English
- Device type: All supported devices
- Business verticals: All advertiser verticals except sensitive categories, such as pharmaceuticals
Pharmaceuticals is the only excluded category the page names. Google does not list the others it treats as sensitive for this feature, so whether categories such as financial services, gambling or healthcare services beyond pharmaceuticals are covered is not stated.
Serving is conditional on Google's own forecast. "Google only showcases review summaries when it's predicted to improve ad performance," the page states under benefits, and repeats under key considerations: "Review summaries only show when predicted to benefit your ad performance." The document does not define which performance measure the prediction targets, whether click-through rate, conversion rate or something else, or whether the prediction is made per auction, per query or per account.
What advertisers cannot do
The control question receives a direct answer. "Because review summaries represent user feedback, advertisers cannot directly edit or customize the generated text," according to Google.
The page closes with a related link to Google's article on account-level automated assets, the family of ad components Google generates itself, such as dynamic sitelinks and seller ratings, which advertisers can usually disable at account level. The review summaries page does not state that review summaries belong to that family, or that the account-level automated asset controls apply to them. Nor does the Help Center's own AI agent box resolve it: one of the suggested questions it surfaces on the page reads "How do I enable AI review summaries for my Search ads?", a question the page itself never answers.
Benefits claimed by Google
Google lists four benefits. Advertisers will "Build customer trust" by displaying "positive user insights from across the web," according to the page. They will "Improve click quality" by providing relevant details before a click, "attracting qualified leads who are more likely to engage." The third benefit is "Improve ad performance," which restates the predictive serving rule. The fourth, "Brand trust," promises to "Strengthen brand trust at the moment of consideration to help turn ad clicks into customer conversions."
None of these claims is accompanied by a figure. The page cites no test results, no uplift in click-through rate, no conversion data and no case study. Google often publishes such numbers with new ad formats; their absence here leaves the performance case resting entirely on Google's description.
A format that has been in testing for almost a year
The documentation follows a string of sightings in live search results. PPC News Feed has tracked them since late 2025.
On December 3, 2025, PPC News Feed reported a section in Search ads that displayed review excerpts, which it said appeared to come from store ratings and showed up mostly on e-commerce ads. Anthony Higman had shared the find on LinkedIn.
On July 3, 2026, a different variant appeared: AI-generated summaries placed just below the ad description, carrying a disclaimer that read "Google AI responses are generated independently and can make mistakes, so double-check responses," according to PPC News Feed. Darcy Burk spotted it, and Search Engine Roundtable also covered it. That version summarised the advertiser more generally rather than reviews specifically, and it attracted scepticism about accuracy.
By August, according to PPC News Feed, a review-focused label reading "What people are saying" was being tested. On September 5, 2026, the outlet reported a further test labelled "What customers love," followed by testimonial-style text, on a sponsored Semrush result. Sachin Patel had shared that example on X.
The help page published this month is the first Google document, among those sources, that describes the feature in its own words, names the markets and states the editing restriction. It does not say whether either label from the tests is the final one, or whether the disclaimer seen in July accompanies the review summaries now. On the same day it reported the help page, PPC News Feed also reported a separate test of a scrolling, marquee-style display of ratings and reviews in sponsored results, which suggests review content in Search ads is still being reworked visually.
Why it matters for advertisers
The change moves a piece of Search ad copy out of the advertiser's hands. Advertisers have, for years, accepted Google-generated components alongside their own text. In February 2024 Google completed the rollout of generative AI in automatically created assets for English-language advertisers in the US and UK, generating headlines and descriptions for responsive search ads and Performance Max. That system was opt-in at campaign level, and advertisers could remove assets they did not want.
Pressure from advertisers for tighter control over generated copy has been visible since. In September 2025, Google introduced text guidelines for Performance Max and AI Max for Search, allowing up to 25 term exclusions and 40 messaging restrictions per campaign. In February 2026, that beta went global across all languages and verticals.
Review summaries sit outside that framework, at least on the evidence of the help page. The page does not mention text guidelines, term exclusions or messaging restrictions, and it justifies the lack of editing on the grounds that the text "represent[s] user feedback." That is a distinct position from automatically created assets, where the generated copy speaks for the advertiser. Here Google presents the text as a summary of third parties' views, compiled by Google, attached to an ad the advertiser pays for.
Accuracy is a practical concern rather than a theoretical one. Research covered by PPC Land in February 2026 found that 47.1% of marketers encounter AI inaccuracies several times each week, and that 36.5% said hallucinated or incorrect AI content had been published publicly, according to an NP Digital survey of 565 US marketers. A misattributed claim in an organic AI Overviews answer is one thing; the same kind of error inside a paid placement, on a business's own ad, lands differently, because the advertiser is paying for the impression and cannot correct the text.
There is also a regulatory backdrop to reviews in advertising. In August 2024, the US Federal Trade Commission finalised a rule targeting fake reviews and testimonials, covering fabricated reviews, undisclosed insider endorsements and the suppression of negative feedback. The help page does not discuss how a positive-only summary compiled by a platform relates to rules written for reviews published by businesses, and Google has not addressed that publicly in the sources available.
Performance context
The feature arrives as Search clicks face new pressure from AI features on the results page. A Seer Interactive study covered by PPC Land in November 2025 found paid click-through rates on queries that triggered AI Overviews fell 68%, from 19.7% to 6.34%, between June 2024 and September 2025. Additional content in the ad unit, if it lifts engagement, would offset part of that decline. Google has not published data showing that review summaries do so.
Search remains Google's largest revenue line. Google Search and other revenue reached $63.271 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up 17% year over year. Any format change applied across all ad positions on Google.com in four English-speaking markets touches a large share of that inventory.
What is not yet known
Several practical questions remain unanswered by the documentation:
- whether advertisers can opt out, and whether the account-level automated asset settings cover the feature;
- which review platforms Google draws from, and whether reviews about competitors or unrelated businesses with similar names can be excluded;
- whether a label or disclaimer identifies the text as AI-generated in the ad itself;
- whether reporting will show when a summary appeared and how it performed;
- which categories beyond pharmaceuticals count as sensitive;
- when the feature became generally available in each of the four markets.
The help page itself carries no date, so the start of availability cannot be established from it.
Timeline
- February 12, 2024 - Google completes the generative AI rollout in automatically created assets for English-language advertisers in the US and UK.
- August 18, 2024 - The US FTC finalises its rule on fake reviews and testimonials, announced August 14, 2024.
- September 10, 2025 - Google introduces text guidelines for AI Max for Search and Performance Max, with 25 term exclusions and 40 messaging restrictions per campaign.
- November 5, 2025 - Seer Interactive study shows paid CTR on AI Overview queries fell 68%.
- December 3, 2025 - PPC News Feed reports AI-powered review snippets in Search ads, spotted by Anthony Higman.
- February 2, 2026 - NP Digital research finds 47.1% of marketers encounter AI errors weekly.
- February 26, 2026 - Text guidelines beta goes global.
- July 3, 2026 - AI-generated summaries with a "can make mistakes" disclaimer appear below Search ad descriptions.
- July 23, 2026 - Google Search revenue reaches $63.271 billion in Q2 2026.
- August 2026 - A review summary test labelled "What people are saying" appears, according to PPC News Feed.
- September 5, 2026 - PPC News Feed reports a "What customers love" review summary test on a Semrush ad.
- Undated - Google publishes the "About Review summaries" help page, covering Search campaigns in the US, UK, Australia and India in English.
- October 24, 2026 - PPC News Feed first reports the help page, crediting Hana Kobzová, and separately reports a scrolling marquee test for ratings and reviews.

- Google introduces text guidelines for AI-powered advertising campaigns - the September 2025 launch of term exclusions and messaging restrictions for generated ad text.
- Google's text guidelines beta goes global for AI Max and Performance Max - the February 2026 worldwide expansion of those controls.
- Nearly half of marketers encounter AI errors weekly as study exposes trust gap - NP Digital's survey and accuracy test of six LLM platforms.

- FTC to combat fake reviews and testimonials - the 2024 US rule on fabricated, undisclosed and suppressed reviews.
- Google Search ads gain 17% to $63.3 billion while network drops 1% - Alphabet's Q2 2026 results.
Summary
Who: Google, advertisers running Search campaigns in the US, UK, Australia and India, and searchers who see their ads. PPC News Feed first reported the documentation, crediting Hana Kobzová.
What: A Google Ads Help page describes AI-generated, positive-only summaries of online reviews that appear inside Search ads. Advertisers cannot edit the text, and Google shows it only when it predicts better ad performance. Sensitive categories such as pharmaceuticals are excluded.
When: The help page is undated. PPC News Feed reported it on October 24, 2026, after test sightings dating back to December 2025.
Where: All ad positions on Google.com, in English, in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and India, on all supported devices.
Why: Google says the summaries build trust and improve click quality and ad performance, but the page publishes no data to support those claims and does not explain opt-out options, review sources or reporting.
